files.lesson.md: --- order: 21 unit: quad9 node: AC9M9A04 n4 uses: [AC9M9A04 n3] assumes: [AC9M9A04 n3] connection: poster-area title: Three ways to solve summary: "The solutions of a quadratic are the zeros in a table, the x-intercepts of a graph and the numbers that make each bracket 0. They are the same numbers seen three ways." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A poster is 4 cm longer than it is wide and covers 45 square centimetres. You could solve it with algebra, a graph or a table. Do they agree?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8368 url: http://127.0.0.1:8368/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- You can solve the same quadratic with a table, a graph or algebra. Each shows the same two numbers in a different way. ## Predict: from the graph to the brackets ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a factorised form from a graph shows who reads the intercepts and then flips the sign, and who copies the intercepts straight into the brackets." check: type: predict q: "The graph of $y = x^2 + 4x - 45$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -9$ and $x = 5$. Which is the factorised form?" options: - "(x + 9)(x − 5)" - "(x − 9)(x + 5)" - "(x − 9)(x − 5)" - "(x + 9)(x + 5)" actual: "(x + 9)(x − 5). Each bracket is 0 at an intercept: x + 9 = 0 at x = −9, and x − 5 = 0 at x = 5. Check: 9 × (−5) = −45 and 9 − 5 = 4." ``` The curve crosses the axis in two places. What do the brackets look like? ## Run: zeros in a table, intercepts on a graph ```step stage: run insight: "The table's zeros and the graph's x-intercepts land on the same x-values, so a table and a graph both find the solutions." try: { playground: board, starter: "three.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $P$ to the left-hand place where the curve meets the $x$-axis. Which value in the table is 0? Was your prediction right?", when: "x(P) = -9 and y(P) = 0" } ``` The table lists $y = x^2 + 4x - 45$ for some $x$-values. Find the zero in the table and on the graph. ## Investigate: connecting the three ```step stage: investigate insight: "A zero in the table, an x-intercept and a bracket that gives 0 are one number seen three ways. A table of whole numbers can miss a solution, so check the graph or the algebra too." tasks: - check: type: number q: "For $y = x^2 + 4x - 45$, what is $y$ when $x = 4$?" answer: -13 explain: "4² + 4 × 4 − 45 = 16 + 16 − 45 = −13." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $4^2 + 4 \\times 4$?", answer: 32, explain: "16 + 16 = 32." } - check: type: question q: "The graph of $y = x^2 - 2x - 8$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -2$ and $x = 4$. Which is its factorised form?" options: ["$(x + 2)(x - 4)$", "$(x - 2)(x + 4)$", "$(x - 2)(x - 4)$", "$(x + 2)(x + 4)$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That gives x = 2 and x = −4: the signs are the wrong way round.", "That gives x = 2 and 4: both positive.", "That gives x = −2 and −4: both negative."] explain: "x = −2 comes from (x + 2) = 0 and x = 4 from (x − 4) = 0." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mei" text: "Mei solves $x^2 + 4x - 45 = 0$ from a table of $x = 0$ to $10$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: table-first-zero-only explain: "Line 3: her table starts at 0, so it can't show the other solution at x = −9. An equation like this has two solutions, so check negatives or use algebra." - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$ by any method. What is the larger solution?" answer: 4 explain: "(x + 2)(x − 4) = 0, so x = −2 or x = 4." ``` ### Same numbers Here's one equation solved three ways. ```worked x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 :: The equation. (x + 2)(x - 4) = 0,\; x = -2 \text{ or } x = 4 :: Algebra: factorise, then each bracket. \text{crosses the x-axis at } -2 \text{ and } 4 :: Graph: the x-intercepts. y = 7, 0, -5, -8, -9, -8, -5, 0, 7 \text{ for } x = -3, -2, \ldots, 5 :: Table: y is 0 at x = −2 and x = 4. -2 \text{ and } 4 :: All three methods give the same numbers. ``` Now try one on paper: $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$. Solve it by factorising and check one solution in a table. Type the smaller solution. ### Graph to brackets ### Find the mistake Read Mei's working. Which line reaches the wrong conclusion? ### Larger solution ## Modify: change the constant ```step stage: modify insight: "Moving the constant c lifts the curve: two solutions, one solution or none. The table shows y = 0 only where the curve meets the axis." try: { playground: board, starter: "three.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - hint: ["The curve is y = x² − 4x + c.", "For crossings at 1 and 3: (x − 1)(x − 3) = x² − 4x + 3."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $c$ so the curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.", when: "c = 3" } - hint: ["Make the curve just touch the axis.", "How many solutions is that?"] check: { type: question, q: "When $c = 4$ the curve just touches the $x$-axis at $x = 2$. How many solutions does $x^2 - 4x + 4 = 0$ have?", options: ["One: x = 2", "Two", "None", "Three"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The curve touches the axis once, so the two brackets give the same answer.", "It does touch the axis, at x = 2.", "A quadratic has at most two."], explain: "x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)(x − 2), so x = 2 is the only solution." } - hint: ["Set c = 5 and look at the table.", "Does y ever equal 0?"] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: when $c = 5$ the curve stays above the $x$-axis. How many solutions does $x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0$ have?", options: ["None: y is never 0", "Two", "One", "It depends on x"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Two solutions need two crossings.", "One solution needs the curve to touch the axis.", "x doesn't change: the curve never reaches 0."], explain: "The table never shows 0 and the curve never meets the axis, so there are no solutions." } ``` ### Crossing at 1 and 3 ### Touching ### Missing the axis ## Practise: any method ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing the quickest method for each equation and checking with a second one." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 + x - 6 = 0$. What is the smaller solution?" answer: -3 explain: "(x + 3)(x − 2) = 0, so x = −3 or x = 2." - check: type: number q: "For $y = x^2 - 5x + 4$, what is $y$ when $x = 2$?" answer: -2 explain: "4 − 10 + 4 = −2." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $2^2 - 5 \\times 2$?", answer: -6, explain: "4 − 10 = −6." } - check: type: question q: "The table for $y = x^2 - 5x + 4$ shows $y = 0$ at $x = 1$ and $x = 4$. Which equation does that solve?" options: ["$(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$", "$(x + 1)(x + 4) = 0$", "$(x - 1)(x + 4) = 0$", "$(x + 1)(x - 4) = 0$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That gives x = −1 and −4.", "That gives x = 1 and −4.", "That gives x = −1 and 4."] explain: "x = 1 gives (x − 1) = 0 and x = 4 gives (x − 4) = 0." - check: type: number q: "Review: a rectangle is $x$ m wide and $(x + 2)$ m long, area 35 m². The equation gives $x = 5$ or $x = -7$. What is the width in metres?" answer: 5 explain: "A width can't be negative, so x = 5." ``` ### Smaller solution ### A table value ### From table to brackets ### Review From the last lesson: the situation picks the solution. ## Make: the poster ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the poster: solve it with algebra, then check the answer a second way." tasks: - hint: ["Write x(x + 4) = 45 as x² + 4x − 45 = 0.", "Which numbers multiply to −45 and add to 4?"] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The poster is $x$ cm wide and $(x + 4)$ cm long, with area 45 cm². Solve $x(x + 4) = 45$ and type the width in cm." steps: - ["$x^2 + 4x - 45 = 0$", "make one side 0"] - ["$(x + 9)(x - 5) = 0$", "9 × −5 = −45 and 9 − 5 = 4"] - ["$x = -9 \\text{ or } x = 5$", "each bracket gives a solution"] - ["$x = 5$", "a width can't be negative"] answer: "5" answerLabel: "Width (cm)" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["9", "That's the other number in the bracket: it gives x = −9."] - ["-9", "That solves the equation but a width can't be negative."] criteria: - "I made one side 0 before factorising." - "I chose the solution that fits a width." - "I checked my answer a second way." explain: "x = 5: the poster is 5 cm wide and 9 cm long, with area 45 cm²." - check: type: number q: "Check with the table: what is $x^2 + 4x - 45$ when $x = 5$?" answer: 0 explain: "25 + 20 − 45 = 0, so x = 5 is a zero of the table." ``` ### The width Back to the poster. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Check it The poster size here is made up for the task. **Also used in** - **Design.** Sizes of signs, screens and frames are often set by an area and a ratio, and give quadratic equations. - **Spreadsheets.** A table of values made in a spreadsheet is the quickest way to hunt for a zero. - **Next unit step.** Modelling a real change, and deciding whether a straight line or a curve fits it better. ```teacher summary: "Students solve a quadratic with algebra, a graph and a table, and connect the three: zeros in the table, x-intercepts and factors are the same numbers (AC9M9A04, node 4)." time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 14 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 15 min goals: - I can find the solutions of a quadratic from a table. - I can read the solutions from the x-intercepts of a graph. - I can say how the three ways match the factors. struggle: "Matching a graph's intercepts to the signs in the brackets. Ask: what x makes this bracket 0?" before: > Students need Solving by factorising and Graphing a quadratic. The one idea: the solutions are the same numbers whether you read them from a table, a graph or the brackets. The common mistake is stopping at the first zero in a table and missing the other (Mei's working). The poster's size is made up for the task. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose (x − 9)(x + 5) copied the intercepts into the brackets without flipping the signs." - "Run: ask students to say which x gives 0 in the table and where it is on the graph." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the poster in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for each method named." - "Modify: before the edge cases, ask how many times the curve will cross the axis." stuck: - see: A student writes (x − 9)(x + 5) for crossings at −9 and 5. ask: What x makes (x − 9) zero? fix: x = 9, not −9. Use (x + 9)(x − 5). - see: A student reports one solution from a table. ask: Could there be a zero outside the table? fix: Extend the table to negatives or use algebra. stretch: Find c so that y = x² − 6x + c touches the x-axis once. support: A printed table already filled in, with the zeros circled, to match with the graph. leads: > Continues AC9M9A04 node 4. Where it leads: deciding whether a change is linear or quadratic and modelling it (next). exit: q: A graph crosses the x-axis at 1 and 7. Write the equation in factorised form. a: (x − 1)(x − 7) = 0. explain: > The solutions of a quadratic equation are the zeros of its table, the x-intercepts of its graph and the numbers that make each bracket 0. They are the same numbers seen three ways. A table of whole numbers can miss one, so check with a second method. ```

widget: graph

snap: 1

# endregion

widget: graph
